Neonatal development in the common brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula) begins with a remarkably brief gestation period. Under the standard thermal conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the gestation time is only 17 days [tg = 17 days], one of the shortest recorded for any mammal of comparable adult size. This incredibly rapid intrauterine development results in a highly altricial newborn. The wet weight at birth is a mere 0.279 grams [Wwb = 0.279 grams], a value that corrects the often-cited but erroneous figure of 2 grams found in some general references (Gemmell and Nelson, 1988). This minuscule neonate, essentially a tiny embryo, must immediately undertake an arduous climb from the birth canal to the mother's pouch, where it will attach to a teat for an extended period of continuous suckling. The newborn's diminutive size and profoundly underdeveloped state at parturition represent an extreme altricial strategy, allowing the mother a very low energetic investment during gestation itself.

The period of pouch life in Trichosurus vulpecula is a critical phase of growth and differentiation, culminating in nutritional independence. The time since birth at weaning is 204 days [tx = 204 days] when measured at the species' typical core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This lengthy period in the pouch allows the altricial neonate to complete most of its organogenesis and somatic development. By the time of weaning, the young possum has achieved a substantial wet weight at weaning of 740 grams [Wwx = 740 grams], representing a roughly 2,650-fold increase from its birth mass. At this point, the juvenile begins to exit the pouch for short periods, initially remaining close to the mother, and transitions to a diet of solid food, leaves, and flowers, although it may continue to suckle intermittently for some weeks thereafter.

Sexual maturation in the common brushtail possum exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in timing. For females, the time since birth at puberty is 315 days [tp = 315 days] at a body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], meaning a young female born in the spring could potentially reach reproductive maturity by the following autumn of the same year. Males, however, follow a much slower developmental trajectory. The time since birth at puberty for males is 730 days [tp = 730 days] under identical thermal conditions, a delay of over a year relative to females. This divergence is likely driven by the intense intrasexual competition among males for access to estrous females; the additional year allows males to attain a larger body size and greater social dominance before entering the breeding population.

The common brushtail possum maintains a modest but stable reproductive output that is characteristic of a capital breeder in a seasonal environment. While individual litters are invariably singletons, females can produce approximately 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters per year]. Because each litter contains only one offspring [N_R_i = each litter contains only one offspring], the annual reproductive output is limited, but the species compensates through a long breeding season and high juvenile survival under favorable conditions. This suite of life-history traits—tiny altricial neonates, a brief gestation of 17 days [tg = 17 days], a long pouch residency of 204 days [tx = 204 days], and a low but consistent annual fecundity—suggests a strategy oriented toward steady recruitment rather than high annual productivity at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C].

The maximum recorded longevity of Trichosurus vulpecula indicates a relatively long-lived marsupial for its body size. At a core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the maximum known lifespan is 15.9 years [am = 15.9 years], a substantial duration that allows for multiple years of reproductive activity. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a correspondingly large adult body size. Under favorable conditions, the ultimate wet weight attained by adults is 2395 grams [Wwi = 2395 grams], with males typically reaching the upper end of this range due to their prolonged growth period before puberty. The combination of a long lifespan, a modest annual reproductive rate of approximately 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters per year] with a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and a considerable adult body mass of nearly 2.4 kilograms (2395 grams) [Wwi = 2395 grams] positions the brushtail possum as a slow-lived, K-selected species among arboreal marsupials.
